title: THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE ABOUT GOD’S GRACE IS THE ONE THAT MAKES YOU COMFORTABLE IN YOUR SIN
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE ABOUT GOD’S GRACE IS THE ONE THAT MAKES YOU COMFORTABLE IN YOUR SIN

Jude warned about people who turned the mercy of Jesus Christ into permission to live however they pleased. Nearly 2,000 years later, that warning may be more urgent than ever. Because the greatest danger isn't always someone telling you to abandon Jesus. Sometimes it's someone convincing you that you can keep Jesus while refusing to surrender the very sin He died to save you from.
There is a kind of preaching that makes people feel safe while their souls are drifting further from God.
It sounds compassionate.
It sounds liberating.
It uses beautiful words like grace, freedom, acceptance, love, and forgiveness.
And some of those words are among the most precious truths in the entire Bible.
But something terrible happens when those truths are separated from repentance, holiness, and the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Grace becomes an excuse.
Freedom becomes a disguise.
And the cross becomes something people celebrate with their mouths while refusing to let its message confront their lives.
The frightening part?
A person can become comfortable with that kind of Christianity without ever realizing what has happened.
They can sing worship songs on Sunday, quote Scripture on Monday, encourage someone else on Tuesday, and return to the same deliberately protected sin by Wednesday.
And whenever conviction begins to rise, they whisper something that sounds spiritual enough to silence it.
“God understands.”
“I'm only human.”
“Nobody is perfect.”
“Jesus already forgave me.”
But what happens when the truth of God's forgiveness becomes the excuse we use to avoid His call to repentance?
What happens when we begin treating the blood of Jesus as permission to continue doing what nailed Him to the cross?
That is not a new question.
Nearly two thousand years ago, a servant of Jesus Christ named Jude confronted this very danger.
And his warning was so serious that it deserves more than a quick reading.
It deserves an examination of our hearts.
Jude wrote:

“For certain men crept in privily, even they who were of old written of beforehand unto this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.”
— Jude 4, American Standard Version (1901)
Read that again.
Not people who openly announced that they hated God.
Not necessarily people who entered the church carrying obvious signs of rebellion.
People who crept in unnoticed.
People who could move among believers while corrupting the meaning of grace.
People who took something holy and used it to justify something unholy.
And Jude wanted the church to recognize the danger before it spread.
In the original Greek, the expression translated “turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” includes these words:
τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριτα μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν
Tēn tou theou hēmōn charita metatithentes eis aselgeian.
The word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, or a gift of kindness. In this passage, it refers to God's grace, which these ungodly people were misusing.

The participle μετατιθέντες (metatithentes) comes from a verb meaning to change, transfer, or alter. Jude is describing people who were perverting grace by turning it toward a purpose completely opposed to its true meaning.
And the word ἀσέλγεια (aselgeia) refers to sensuality, licentiousness, or shameless conduct. It is a term associated with behavior that disregards moral restraint, often including sexual immorality.
Jude was not merely warning about people who struggled with temptation.
He was confronting people who twisted God's grace into a justification for ungodliness.
That distinction matters.
Because there is an enormous difference between a believer who hates the sin they keep falling into and someone who has decided that grace means they no longer need to fight it.
One is wounded and needs restoration.
The other is defending the very thing from which Christ calls us to turn.
And sometimes, if we are painfully honest, we have stood somewhere between those two realities.
We knew something was wrong.
We felt conviction.
We promised God we would change.
Then temptation came again.
The private conversation.
The hidden relationship.
The pornography nobody knew about.
The dishonest transaction.
The bitterness we kept feeding.
The gossip we disguised as concern.
The addiction we insisted we could control.
The secret life that looked nothing like the person everyone saw at church.
And after everything, we told ourselves that grace would cover it.
Now hear this carefully.
God's grace truly is sufficient for the sinner who comes to Christ. But His grace was never given to make peace with the sin that is destroying us.
The apostle Paul confronted the same distortion.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. We who died to sin, how shall we any longer live therein?”
— Romans 6:1–2, ASV
In Greek, Paul's rejection begins with:
μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
An emphatic expression meaning, in this context, “Absolutely not!” or “May it never be!”
Paul was not uncertain.
He did not suggest that continued sin was simply an unfortunate but acceptable consequence of abundant grace.
He rejected the entire idea.
Why?
Because grace does not merely change our standing before God.
Grace also changes our relationship with sin.
The gospel announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ, and it calls forgiven people into a new life.
Not a life of instant perfection.
Not a life without temptation.
Not a life where believers never stumble.
But a life in which sin is no longer defended as our rightful master.
This is where the message becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us are not struggling to understand what the Bible says.
We are struggling to surrender what we already know God is asking us to leave behind.
We want forgiveness without confession.
Comfort without correction.
Resurrection without the death of our old ways.
A Savior who rescues us from judgment, but not a Lord who has authority over our choices.
And yet Jesus never presented discipleship that way.
He said:
“If any man would come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
— Luke 9:23, ASV
Daily.
Not just when worship music makes us emotional.
Not just when the sermon speaks directly to our circumstances.
Not just when life falls apart and we suddenly remember how desperately we need God.
Daily.
There is a cross-shaped surrender that belongs to following Jesus.
And it is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like deleting a number you keep returning to.
Sometimes it looks like confessing the truth after months of pretending.
Sometimes it looks like walking away from money you could have gained dishonestly.
Sometimes it means asking forgiveness from someone you have spent years blaming.
Sometimes it means admitting that the thing you call a harmless habit has become a master.
Sometimes it means closing the door to a relationship you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
And sometimes it means kneeling beside your bed with tears in your eyes, finally saying:
“Lord, I don't want to keep defending this anymore. I need You to change me.”
That is not the death of grace.
That is what grace can begin to produce in a surrendered heart.
But perhaps someone reading this has already begun to feel afraid.
Because you know your own failures.
You know how many times you have made promises.
You remember the prayers you prayed with trembling sincerity, only to find yourself battling the same temptation again.
And now a question is rising inside you.
Have I gone too far?
Have I abused God's grace too many times?
Is Jesus tired of me?
Before fear convinces you to run from Him, remember something essential.
Jude's warning was not written to teach broken sinners that Jesus refuses to receive the repentant.
It was written to protect the church from those who corrupt the truth about God's grace.
And the same Bible that warns against turning grace into license also reveals the breathtaking mercy of Christ toward those who return to Him.
Consider Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard the teachings.
He had promised loyalty.
And when the moment of testing came, Peter denied knowing the Lord.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the weight of that memory.
The sound of his own voice.
The fear.
The shame.
The terrible realization that the courage he thought he possessed had collapsed when it mattered.
Luke records that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Christ confronted Peter not to destroy him, but to call him again into love and service.
“Feed my sheep.”
Those words were not permission for Peter to keep denying Jesus.
They were a commission from the Savior who had not finished working in him.
That is the difference between grace and permission.
Permission says, “Stay where you are. Nothing needs to change.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ. Your failure does not have to be the end.”
And perhaps that is exactly what someone needs to hear today.
Your past does not have to write your future.
Your worst decision does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your shame does not have to become your home.
But neither does the mercy of Jesus give you a reason to remain chained to what He calls you to abandon.
Jesus does not forgive us because sin is harmless. He forgives us because His mercy is greater than the guilt of those who turn to Him.
And that mercy came at a cost beyond anything we could ever repay.
Think about Calvary.
Not as a religious symbol you have seen so many times that it no longer moves you.
Think about the real suffering of the Son of God.
The betrayal.
The abandonment.
The mocking.
The scourging.
The cross.
The darkness of that hour.
The innocent Christ bearing our sins.
Peter wrote:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his body upon the tree, that we, having died unto sins, might live unto righteousness; by whose stripes ye were healed.”
— 1 Peter 2:24, ASV
Notice both parts.
He bore our sins.
And the purpose includes that we might live unto righteousness.
Forgiveness and transformation belong together in the saving work of Jesus.
We are not made righteous before God by achieving moral perfection through our own strength.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.
Grace is the source.
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are part of the life God prepares for those He saves.
That is why Titus 2:11–12 is so important.

“For the grace of God hath appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us, to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly and righteously and godly in this present world.”
— Titus 2:11–12, ASV
Do you see it?
Grace instructs us.
Grace trains us.
Grace teaches us to reject ungodliness.
The same grace that welcomes the repentant sinner also teaches that sinner to turn away from the old life.
And that means conviction is not always evidence that God has abandoned you.
Sometimes conviction is the very warning you desperately needed to stop walking toward destruction.
There is a difference between condemnation that drives you into despair and godly sorrow that leads you toward repentance.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 7:10 that godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, while worldly sorrow produces death.
One leaves us trapped in hopelessness.
The other turns us toward God.
So when the Word exposes something in your life, do not automatically mistake that exposure for rejection.
Ask whether the Lord is calling you to bring into the light what you have kept hidden.
Because the enemy would love for you to choose one of two terrible extremes.
Either become so comfortable with sin that you no longer repent.
Or become so consumed by shame that you no longer believe Christ will receive you.
Both can keep a person from coming honestly to Jesus.
But the gospel calls us away from both.
It tells the self-righteous that they need mercy.
It tells the guilty that mercy is available in Christ.
It calls the rebellious to repent.
And it calls the despairing to trust the Savior.
John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9, ASV
Not because our confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because tears are payment.
Not because we have finally punished ourselves enough.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
And genuine confession does not merely seek relief from consequences.
It agrees with God about the seriousness of sin and turns toward His mercy.
There is a Greek word often associated with repentance in the New Testament:
μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means repentance, involving a change of mind and outlook that turns a person toward God and away from sin.
Biblical repentance is deeper than feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you did.
It is deeper than regretting the consequences.
It is a changed response to God, expressed in turning from sin and toward Him.
And here is the beautiful truth.
You cannot manufacture a new heart by sheer willpower.
You need the transforming work of God.
That is why the gospel is not merely a message about trying harder.
It is the good news of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, saving sinners and bringing them into new life.
The same Savior who commands repentance also gives His people the Holy Spirit.
And the Spirit produces fruit that human performance alone cannot create.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Meekness.
Self-control.
These are not trophies for people who have never struggled.
They are evidence of God's transforming work in the lives of those who belong to Christ.
And transformation often happens through difficult, ordinary obedience.
One honest confession.
One temptation resisted.
One act of reconciliation.
One prayer offered when you feel spiritually dry.
One decision to seek wise pastoral counsel or accountability instead of hiding.
One more day of trusting Jesus when the battle has not yet ended.
Maybe nobody applauds.
Maybe nobody notices.
Maybe you are still healing from damage you caused or suffering consequences that forgiveness does not immediately erase.
But faithfulness is not meaningless simply because it happens in private.
God sees what others cannot.
And the Christian life is not sustained by pretending we are strong.
It is sustained by abiding in Christ.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
“Apart from me ye can do nothing.”
That truth humbles us.
And it gives us hope.
Because if spiritual transformation depended entirely on our ability to repair ourselves, none of us would have reason to boast or confidence to endure.
But our hope rests in the living Christ.
Now return to Jude.
His warning is especially striking because the letter begins by addressing believers as those who are called, beloved in God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ.
And near the end, Jude urges them to build themselves up in their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ unto eternal life.
He also commands them to show mercy to those who doubt and to seek the rescue of others in spiritual danger, exercising discernment and caution.
Jude was not promoting a cruel Christianity that delights in humiliating struggling people.
He was calling believers to contend for the faith while showing mercy and taking sin seriously.
Truth and mercy were never meant to become enemies.
A church that speaks of holiness without the mercy of Christ can crush the wounded.
A church that speaks of mercy while refusing to confront sin can leave the wounded in danger.
But a church faithful to Jesus must proclaim both.
The holiness of God.
The seriousness of sin.
The sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
The necessity of repentance.
The freedom of forgiveness.
And the transforming power of grace.
This is the message our generation desperately needs.
Not a gospel rewritten to make everyone comfortable.
Not a religion built on fear, performance, and spiritual appearances.
But the real gospel.
The one that exposes sin without denying the possibility of restoration.
The one that humbles the proud and lifts the repentant.
The one that announces that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.
And the one that never confuses being saved from sin with being granted permission to cherish it.
Perhaps this article found you at a moment when your heart is tired of pretending.
You have become skilled at saying, “I'm fine.”
Your family thinks you're strong.
Your friends see the encouraging posts.
People at church know your smile.
But there is a battle behind that smile.
Something you have not surrendered.
Something you are afraid to confess.
Something you keep promising will be the last time.
And deep down, you wonder whether the person everyone admires would still be loved if the truth came out.
Listen.
Jesus already knows the truth about you.
Nothing hidden in your heart surprises Him.
And the invitation of the gospel is not to become a convincing actor.
It is to come into the light.
Not every struggle should be exposed publicly, and wisdom matters when deciding whom to trust with painful details. But you do not have to keep defending darkness in order to protect an image.
You can confess to God.
You can seek help from a mature and trustworthy believer.
You can pursue accountability.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can begin taking real steps away from the sin that has been ruling your decisions.
And when you fall, you do not need to pretend the fall was harmless.
You can return to Christ in repentance, remembering that His mercy is not exhausted by the weakness of those who sincerely seek Him.
This is why I want to ask you something.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not to force a public confession.
But because someone else reading the comments may be carrying the same private battle.
Are you fighting a sin you once tried to justify, but now desperately want Jesus to help you overcome?
And if God is teaching you that repentance is not the end of hope but the beginning of restoration, share a little of what He has been teaching you.
You do not need to reveal private details.
You do not need to perform your pain for strangers.
But your honest testimony may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone and that the door of repentance is still open.
This is also why the mission of Gospel Warrior matters to us.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who will never voluntarily walk into a church building.
People carrying shame.
People questioning whether God can forgive them.
People who have heard a distorted gospel.
People who have been hurt by religious hypocrisy.
People who believe Christianity is either a list of impossible rules or a promise that nothing they do matters.
And somewhere among them is a person who may encounter the truth of Jesus Christ through an article someone cared enough to share.
Think about that.
Tagging a family member or friend who needs encouragement may open a meaningful conversation.
Saving this article may give you something to revisit when temptation tries to persuade you that grace and holiness have nothing to do with each other.
Following Gospel Warrior means you can continue receiving Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, and reminders of the hope found in Christ.
Not because a social media page can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because faithful witnesses can point others toward Him.
And that is the heart behind the Gospel Warrior mission.
We want to keep creating resources that bring people back to the Word of God.
We want to help believers grow beyond inspirational quotations into genuine biblical understanding.
We want people to know not only that Jesus forgives, but also what it means to follow Him.

These resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible to more people, including those who may not have the financial means to purchase books or study materials.
But continuing and expanding this work takes time, labor, and practical resources.
That is why I want to speak openly about something.
The Bible teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
“Let each man do according as he hath purposed in his heart: not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, ASV
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through an opportunity to help sustain and expand work that seeks to honor Jesus Christ.
If you want to glorify God through supporting faithful gospel-centered ministry, this is one practical way you can participate.
These products are simply an added thank-you.
The greater purpose is the mission.
The opportunity to help someone encounter the truth.
To encourage a weary believer.
To challenge a heart growing comfortable with compromise.
To remind a broken person that Jesus Christ still saves and restores.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your response to Jesus.
Because this message is not ultimately about a ministry.
It is not about a platform.
It is not about building an audience.
It is about the Savior who died and rose again so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
And that brings us back to the question Jude forces every generation to confront.
Have we received God's grace as the gift that saves and transforms us, or have we begun using the language of grace to protect what God is calling us to surrender?
There is no benefit in answering that question for someone else while refusing to answer it for ourselves.
It is easy to see compromise in the world.
It is easy to criticize the hypocrisy of public figures.
It is easy to condemn the sins that do not personally tempt us.
But what about the ones that do?
What about the private compromises?
The carefully managed appearances?
The sins we excuse because they are familiar?
The things we would tell another believer to abandon while quietly making exceptions for ourselves?
The Word of God does not permit us to stand above others as though we have no need of mercy.
We all need Christ.
And that is precisely why the gospel is such good news.
The cross does not tell us that our sin was insignificant.
It tells us that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The empty tomb declares that death did not have the final word.
And the invitation to repent reminds us that we do not have to keep living under the dominion of the very things from which Christ came to save us.
Maybe your next step is not another promise made in a moment of emotion.
Maybe it is honest surrender.
Maybe it is confessing the truth to God without excuses.
Maybe it is seeking help.
Maybe it is finally making the difficult decision you have postponed for months.
Maybe it is trusting Jesus again after shame has convinced you that you are beyond His mercy.
Whatever your circumstances, do not confuse grace with permission to remain in rebellion.
And do not confuse repentance with earning salvation.
Come to Jesus.
Not with a polished performance.
Not with a list of reasons your sin should be overlooked.
Not with confidence in your ability to change yourself.
Come with faith in the crucified and risen Lord.
Come acknowledging your need.
Come asking for mercy.
Come willing to follow Him.
And remember how Jude ends his letter.
After warnings about false teachers, corruption, judgment, and spiritual danger, he lifts the eyes of believers toward the One who is able to preserve them.

“Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling, and to set you before the presence of his glory without blemish in exceeding joy, to the only God our Saviour, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion and power, before all time, and now, and for evermore. Amen.”
— Jude 24–25, ASV
What an ending.
Jude does not leave believers staring helplessly at the danger.
He points them to the power of God.
The God who calls His people to holiness is also able to keep them.
The Savior who exposes sin is the Savior who offers forgiveness.
The Lord who commands surrender is the Lord who gives grace to those who depend on Him.
And the final hope of the Christian is not that we were strong enough to save ourselves.
It is that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
So tonight, or whenever these words reach you, perhaps you can make this your prayer:

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have used Your mercy as an excuse instead of receiving it with gratitude and repentance. Show me what I have been hiding, what I have been defending, and what I need to surrender. I cannot change my heart by my own strength. Teach me to trust You, obey Your Word, and walk by Your Spirit. Restore what sin has damaged, give me courage to make things right where I can, and help me remember that Your grace is not permission to remain in darkness. You are my Savior and my Lord. Lead me in Your truth. Amen.”
Not because typing those words saves you.
Not because a public comment proves repentance.
But because sometimes an honest declaration can encourage someone else to seek the Lord as well.
Above all, let the words become a genuine prayer expressed in a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
Because the most beautiful story is not the one where a sinner learns to make sin look acceptable.
It is the one where a sinner discovers that the grace of Jesus is powerful enough to forgive, restore, and begin making all things new.
The scandal was never that Jesus welcomed sinners; the scandal is when we use His welcome as a reason to refuse the transformation He offers.
